blocks.md: **Including part-time and part-year workers, US hourly wages spread out at every percentile from 1974 to 1988. Afterwards the top and the bottom both gained relative to the middle: the 90th percentile ended ≈0.38 log points above 1974, while the 10th, which had fallen behind the median in the 1980s, caught up.**
All values read off the lecture charts, approximate.

sections.heading: Cumulative log change since 1974 (males and females)
Growth at each percentile relative to the median

blocks.md: Log change at percentile $p$ minus log change at the median (three-year moving averages; self-employed and military excluded).

| Group | 1974–1988 | 1988–2008 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Males | Rising line: ≈ −0.15 to −0.2 at the 5th percentile up to ≈ +0.15 at the 95th | U shape: bottom roughly level with the median, slight dip around the 20th–30th, rising to ≈ +0.15 at the 95th |
| Females | Rising line: ≈ −0.2 at the 5th up to ≈ +0.15 at the 95th | Bottom roughly unchanged relative to the median, rising to ≈ +0.15 at the top |

- **Sample matters**: full-time, full-year samples (the usual March CPS cut) miss many low-wage workers; this sample includes them, which is why the lower tail looks different from [US Wage Percentiles 1963-2008](note:us-wage-percentiles-1963-2008).
- **Hourly vs weekly**: these are hourly wages, so changes in hours do not show up as wage changes.
- The pattern matches the within-group facts: falling variance in low-education groups, rising in college groups ([US Within-Education Wage Variance 1973-2009](note:us-within-education-wage-variance-1973-2009)).
